title: Multiplication principle and combinations
transcript: For a recipe with several separate choices, multiply the numbers of choices when every choice in one stage can go with every choice in the next. For a team the order of selection usually does not matter. Use a list or divide out the orders that describe the same team.

AMC Upper Primary practice may ask how many designs or teams can be made. Look for distinct stages of choice, then ask what makes a final outcome different. A Rossmoyne style challenge can restrict the number chosen from each group. Split by group totals before multiplying.
A stall has five flavours and four toppings. You order one of each, and every pairing is allowed. How many different flavour-and-topping orders are possible?

For each flavour there are four different toppings. Listing one row per flavour creates equal row lengths. Multiply by the five flavours, giving twenty combinations. Each order has one flavour and one topping.
Pick an unlabelled pair of helpers from seven students. The two students have the same job and no student can be chosen twice. How many different pairs are possible?
Count an ordered first and second pick. There are seven first choices and six second choices after each one. Every team appears in two orders. Halve the ordered count to get twenty-one teams.

There are six artists, five builders and three coders. Choose four people with either two or three artists and at most one coder. People belong to one group each, and the team has no named roles. How many different teams are possible?

With two artists, the other two can be two builders or one builder and one coder. There are fifteen artist pairs in either case. With three artists, the fourth can be a builder or a coder. There are twenty ways to choose the three artists. Within one row, multiply the choices from different groups. Between rows, add, because each team fits exactly one group pattern.

The four row totals are one hundred and fifty, two hundred and twenty-five, one hundred and sixty. Their sum is five hundred and thirty-five teams. Check that selecting zero coders was allowed, and that you used both allowed artist totals. Those choices account for all four patterns.

Switching two people on a team without named jobs leaves the same team. Count both orders only when the roles differ. You can multiply choices that make up one outcome. Distinct allowable patterns for a whole team are alternatives, so add them.

Decide whether the objects have named positions. Write a short group pattern before calculating individual choices. Multiply the compatible choices within a pattern. Then add the pattern totals after checking each team can fit only one.
